history.answer: Doctor, I have this sharp, stabbing pain in my right heel whenever I take my first steps out of bed in the morning.
It started gradually about two months ago as a dull ache, but over the last few weeks it has become much sharper and more painful.
The pain is right on the bottom of my right heel, slightly toward the inner side, and it does not travel anywhere else.
It feels like a sharp, lancinating pain, like stepping on a nail, and it reaches about a 7 out of 10 during those first steps.
The first five or six steps right after getting out of bed are the most excruciating, and then it slowly eases off.
The sharp morning pain lasts ten to fifteen minutes before settling into a dull ache, though it flares up again toward late afternoon.
Standing up after sitting for a while or walking for a long time makes it worse, but gentle walking initially loosens it up.
No, I do not have any numbness, burning, or pins and needles in my heel, foot, or toes.
No, I have not noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth anywhere on my foot or ankle.
No, it does not wake me up at night, and it doesn't hurt when I am lying resting in bed.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss.
No, I have not twisted my ankle, had any falls, or suffered any direct injury to my foot.
No, the pain is strictly underneath my heel; the back of my heel and my Achilles tendon feel completely normal.
I have never had pain like this in my heels before, and I haven't had any X-rays or other scans done yet.
I tried taking over-the-counter ibuprofen and putting an ice pack on it, which helped a tiny bit, but the morning pain keeps coming back.
I teach middle school, so I spend six to seven hours every day standing and walking across hard classroom floors.
I run four to five miles three days a week, and recently I increased my training mileage to prepare for a 10K race.
I usually wear flat-soled slip-on shoes at work, and my running shoes are quite old and heavily worn down.
It makes teaching very exhausting, and I have had to stop running entirely because of the morning pain.
I was wondering if I developed a bone spur on my heel or badly bruised the bone from running on pavement.
I'm really worried I won't be able to stay on my feet all day to teach my classes.
I was hoping to get an X-ray to see if there's a spur and maybe a recommendation for good shoe inserts.
I have high blood pressure and slightly elevated cholesterol, both diagnosed about five years ago.
I had an appendectomy twenty years ago, but I have had no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day every morning for my blood pressure.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked or used tobacco products.
I drink one glass of red wine once or twice a week with dinner.
I work as a school teacher and live in a two-story home with my husband and two teenage children.
My mother has high blood pressure and my father had a heart attack in his seventies, but there is no family history of joint diseases.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, and my monthly cycles are completely regular.
There is no possibility of pregnancy because my husband had a vasectomy several years ago.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
The patient is alert, well-appearing, and walks into the examination room with an antalgic gait favoring her right heel.
No erythema, ecchymosis, warmth, callus, puncture wounds, or skin breakdown on the right foot or heel.

Exquisite localized tenderness upon palpation of the right medial calcaneal tubercle and plantar fascia insertion, exacerbated by passive great toe dorsiflexion; normal ankle range of motion without effusion.
Mild gastrocnemius tightness on the right, but no tenderness along the Achilles tendon or retrocalcaneal bursa, and Thompson test is negative.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with prompt capillary refill under two seconds.
Light touch and pinprick sensation intact across the plantar surface and toes, with a negative Tinel sign at the tarsal tunnel.
Full 5/5 motor strength on ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion, and eversion bilaterally.
Antalgic gait with shortened right stance phase and avoidance of full right heel strike.
